name: Battle of Sekigahara
info: On 21 October 1600 the forces of Tokugawa Ieyasu defeated a coalition led by Ishida Mitsunari in what is now Gifu Prefecture after several commanders defected; Ieyasu became shōgun in 1603.

facts.date: 21 October 1600 (Keichō 5, 15th day of the 9th month); the start is put at about 08:00 by tradition and closer to 10:00 by recent Japanese research
facts.place: Sekigahara, a narrow basin between Mount Nangu and Mount Matsuo, in what is now Gifu Prefecture, Japan
facts.sides: The Eastern Army under Tokugawa Ieyasu, with Ii Naomasa as supreme field commander, against the Western Army, a coalition formally led by Mōri Terumoto and led in the field by Ishida Mitsunari on behalf of the child Toyotomi Hideyori. Ii's unit numbered 3,600 and the defecting Kobayakawa forces over 15,000.
facts.outcome: The Eastern Army won after Kobayakawa Hideaki and other Western commanders changed sides. Mitsunari was captured and executed on 6 November, and about 87 daimyō lost their domains.

t: The Western Army's commanders were divided, and several of them, Kobayakawa Hideaki among them, defected before or during the fighting, so the battle was settled by loyalties as much as by arms.
Recent Japanese research puts the battle at about two hours, from 10:00 to 12:00, not the full day of the Edo period accounts, and doubts the story that Ieyasu fired on Hideaki to force him to act.
The victory gave Ieyasu the authority to redistribute domains worth 6.8 million koku, and in 1603 he was appointed shōgun.
dyk: Tokugawa Ieyasu's own letter of 21 October 1600 to Date Masamune, the primary source for the duration, led the historian Andō Yūichirō to estimate that the battle took only two hours, from 10:00 to 12:00.
ev: Daimyō of the Military Faction march on Ishida Mitsunari's residence, and Ieyasu mediates
Ieyasu asks Uesugi Kagekatsu to explain his military build-up, and Kagekatsu refuses
Mitsunari, Ōtani Yoshitsugu, Ankokuji Ekei and Mashita Nagamori agree to ask Mōri Terumoto to command; he reaches Osaka Castle on 22 August
Mitsunari's Western Army arrives at Ōgaki Castle on 15 September
The two coalitions make contact at Kuisegawa on 20 October, and both move to Sekigahara
The battle of 21 October is fought; Western commanders defect and the Western Army collapses
Mitsunari, Konishi Yukinaga and Ankokuji Ekei are captured and executed on 6 November

sections.background:
Toyotomi Hideyoshi's heir, Toyotomi Hideyori, was only five years old at his death, and the result was a power vacuum. After the Imjin War factions formed between Ishida Mitsunari and seven former Toyotomi generals including Katō Kiyomasa. The death of Maeda Toshiie, a long-term ally of Hideyoshi and Oda Nobunaga who had been sympathetic to Mitsunari, loosened the balance. Tokugawa Ieyasu drew Kiyomasa and Fukushima Masanori to his side, while Mitsunari claimed to act for the Toyotomi. In 1598 several daimyō of the Military Faction marched on Mitsunari's residence, and Ieyasu mediated.

Tensions rose in 1599 over rumoured plots against Ieyasu. Uesugi Kagekatsu, one of Hideyori's regents, built up his army, and when Ieyasu demanded an explanation, Naoe Kanetsugu answered with a mocking letter pointing to Ieyasu's own violations of Hideyoshi's orders. In May 1600 Kagekatsu refused to explain himself, and Ieyasu called his allies to punish the Uesugi.

Mitsunari met Ōtani Yoshitsugu, Mashita Nagamori and Ankokuji Ekei to plan an anti-Tokugawa army, with Mōri Terumoto as overall commander. This coalition came to be called the Western Army, and Terumoto captured Osaka Castle while the main Tokugawa army was marching to suppress Kagekatsu. The Tokugawa-led coalition was the Eastern Army.
sections.forces:
Ieyasu left Edo on 7 October with 30,000 men, and Ii Naomasa's unit, the Ii no Akazonae, numbered 3,600 crimson-clad troops. Ieyasu had bought large quantities of Tanegashima matchlocks, and Spanish accounts record that 19 cannon from the Dutch ship De Liefde were used by the Tokugawa army as field artillery. Large parts of both armies took no part: Tokugawa Hidetada and Sakakibara Yasumasa, with as many as 38,000 soldiers, were held at the Siege of Ueda by the Sanada, and 15,000 Western soldiers were delayed at Tanabe by 500 troops under Hosokawa Yūsai.

Mitsunari had meant to use Gifu Castle, held by Oda Hidenobu, and Ōgaki Castle as choke points, but Gifu Castle was captured by Fukushima Masanori and Ii Naomasa before the main Western forces arrived. Learning that the Tokugawa army was moving towards Osaka, he prepared to fight in the open at Sekigahara.

The field is a narrow basin with Mount Nangu to the south and Mount Matsuo to the north. Stephen Turnbull notes that it forced the Western Army into a linear formation, limiting its numerical advantage, and gave defectors high ground from which to enfilade its lines. Jakob Meckel, a Prussian general who advised Meiji Japan, read a map of the forces and judged that the Western Army, with greater numbers and higher ground, should have won, and was at first sceptical of the Japanese officer who explained how the Eastern Army had.
sections.course:
At dawn on 21 October the Tokugawa advance guard stumbled into Ishida's army in dense fog, and both sides panicked and withdrew, though each now knew where the other stood. Tradition puts the start at about 08:00, but recent Japanese research puts it closer to 10:00. Ii Naomasa, appointed by Ieyasu supreme field commander, attacked the Western centre with his 3,600 men, and Fukushima Masanori followed and engaged Ukita Hideie. The battle then reached a deadlock, which the eyewitness Ōta Gyūichi described as friends and foes pushing each other under thundering gunfire and hails of arrows.

The Western Army then began to fray. Kobayakawa Hideaki, who had agreed beforehand to change sides, attacked Ōtani Yoshitsugu from behind with over 15,000 men according to one contemporary record, and the commanders Wakisaka Yasuharu, Ogawa Suketada, Akaza Naoyasu and Kutsuki Mototsuna also changed sides. Mōri Terumoto's force stayed at Osaka Castle, and Kikkawa Hiroie, who had colluded with the Eastern Army, held up the Mōri troops in front of Mōri Hidemoto and Chōsokabe Morichika.

Ukita Hideie's front gave way, Yoshitsugu killed himself, and Shima Sakon was fatally shot. Shimazu Yoshihiro's troops were surrounded and broke out after devastating casualties with only 200 soldiers left, using a rearguard action later called sutegamari. Andō Yūichirō estimates that the whole battle lasted two hours, from 10:00 to 12:00, and Ieyasu's own letter to Date Masamune supports him.
sections.aftermath:
Ieyasu feared that Mōri Terumoto, with troops still largely intact, would hold Osaka Castle with Hideyori, and persuaded him to leave by promising a peaceful settlement. He then went back on his promise: he gave the Mōri lands to Kikkawa Hiroie, citing seized letters that implied Terumoto's major role in the anti-Tokugawa movement. Hiroie refused and petitioned for Terumoto, and Ieyasu spared the clan on 10 October but cut its holdings from eight provinces to two, Suō and Nagato, worth 298,000 koku. Ōgaki Castle surrendered when news arrived, and its garrison commander was pardoned.

Ieyasu redistributed domains worth 6.8 million koku, mostly to the allies who had helped him, among them Ikeda Terumasa, Fukushima Masanori, Katō Kiyomasa and Kobayakawa Hideaki, who received 520,000 koku. Roughly 87 daimyō lost their domains for supporting Mitsunari. The Chōsokabe lost Tosa, where a revolt of former retainers was put down in five weeks with about 273 killed. Shimazu Yoshihiro's clan negotiated until 1602 and was the only Western Army clan to lose no territory.

Sawayama Castle, Mitsunari's home, fell, and most of his relatives were killed or died by their own hands. On 6 November Mitsunari, Konishi Yukinaga and Ankokuji Ekei were captured and executed. Ieyasu had a burial mound for heads, a Kubizuka, built for those who had fallen. In 1603 Emperor Go-Yōzei appointed him shōgun.
sections.sources:
Most of what is known comes from Japanese chronicles and letters, and from historians who read them. Ōta Gyūichi, who was present, wrote a chronicle, and Nakatomi Yūhan-ki records the Kobayakawa attack. Ieyasu's own letter of 21 October to Date Masamune is a primary source for the timing, and Spanish accounts record the Dutch cannon. The Keichō Kenbunsho preserves Ōtani Yoshitsugu's warning to Mitsunari that he was hated by the daimyō. Hayashi Gahō, writing in 1664 as a Tokugawa historian, praised Ieyasu in terms of martial virtue and the peace he founded, so that later accounts of the battle rest on pro-Tokugawa tradition.

Historians dispute the start (08:00 or 10:00), the length (two hours, against the Edo period view of twice that) and Hideaki's defection. The older tradition has him hesitate until about noon and shows Ieyasu firing arquebuses at his position, a story from an Edo-period anecdote. Jun Shiramine and Junji Mitsunari hold that he had already changed sides before the battle, and Turnbull, Masayuki Fujimoto and Yūichi Goza doubt the shooting, which Goza suggests may be dramatisation by pro-Tokugawa historiography. The Shimazu breakout is also questioned: modern historians caution that the charge of Shimazu Toyohisa, later told as heroic, may be Edo-period embellishment. Some anecdotes, such as Komatsuhime's refusal to admit her father-in-law, may be partly apocryphal.
sections.legacy:
Mitsunari's defeat is generally considered the beginning of the Tokugawa shogunate, which ruled Japan for two and a half centuries until 1868. The battle also shifted the authority to assign ranks and lands from the Toyotomi clan to Ieyasu. Watanabe Daimon suspects the verbal grants of domains reflect Ieyasu's wariness of Hideyori.

Historians explain the result politically. Kasaya Kazuhiko, Mizuno Goki, Watanabe Daimon and others point to the resentment many daimyō, especially veterans of the invasions of Korea, felt towards Mitsunari. Yūichi Goza concludes that Mitsunari overestimated the authority of the Toyotomi, while Toshi Kohara holds that the daimyō thought fighting for Ieyasu served Hideyori's interests best, and Kazuto Hongo calls the campaign more a political than a military victory for Ieyasu. Watanabe cautions that rumours of Mitsunari's slander of Hideaki may reflect a bias that blamed him for everything that went wrong before the battle.

The battlefield was registered as a Monument of Japan in 1931, with the positions of Ieyasu and Mitsunari and the place of Ōtani Yoshitsugu's death marked. The battle appears in Ryōtarō Shiba's novel Sekigahara (1966) and its 2017 film, in James Clavell's Shōgun, and in several video games and television dramas.

summary: At Sekigahara on 21 October 1600 Tokugawa Ieyasu's Eastern Army defeated the Western Army led by Ishida Mitsunari for the child Toyotomi Hideyori, after Kobayakawa Hideaki and others changed sides. The victory gave Ieyasu the power to redistribute domains, and in 1603 he became shōgun.
notes: The article's statistics table (troop counts in tens of thousands) did not survive in the saved text: no army totals, no casualty figures. I gave only the numbers in the prose and said so in the sources section.

The article is inconsistent on dates: it says Ieyasu wrote to Terumoto on 'September 17' and sent an army against Sawayama on 'September 17', before the battle date of October 21; I left both dates out. Gifu Castle falls on 23 August in one place and 29 September in another; I used neither. Kikkawa Hiroie's collusion is 'one day before the battle' in the background but Terumoto's 'defection' is described as keeping his troops at Osaka; both told.
The Kuisegawa contact on 20 October: the chronology says the 'Eastern force retreats to Sekigahara' and the 'Western coalition heads to Sekigahara'.
The article's heading for Ieyasu's rewards includes details of many domains; I gave only the total (6.8 million koku) and four names. Kinoshita Katsutoshi and Miyabe Nagafusa left out.
Date given 'Keichō 5, 15th day of the 9th month' is as in the article (Japanese lunisolar calendar, converted to 21 October 1600 in the article).
